clinicalPearls: Presents as a solitary, slowly growing, often reddish or skin-coloured papule or nodule, classically on the sole or side of the foot.
The palms, and increasingly other sites such as the trunk and head, may also be affected, reflecting derivation from any acrosyringeal duct.
Lesions are frequently vascular in appearance and may sit in a shallow cup-shaped depression with a surrounding keratotic collarette.
They can bleed readily on minor trauma and are commonly mistaken for a pyogenic granuloma or amelanotic melanoma.
Dermoscopy may show polymorphous vessels, a pink-white structureless background and a vascular pattern that overlaps with malignant lesions.
Histology shows a well-demarcated proliferation of small, monomorphous cuboidal poroid cells connected to the epidermis, with ductal differentiation.
Porocarcinoma, the malignant counterpart, may arise de novo or within a long-standing poroma and shows atypia, infiltration and mitoses.
Complete excision with histopathological confirmation is the treatment of choice, given the difficulty of clinical differentiation from malignancy.
reference.pathophysiology: Poroma is a benign adnexal neoplasm arising from the terminal portion of the sweat duct, the acrosyringium, and although traditionally termed eccrine it may show apocrine or folliculosebaceous differentiation. Tumour cells are small, uniform poroid keratinocytes forming broad anastomosing cords connected to the overlying epidermis, punctuated by ductal lumina reflecting the sweat-duct lineage. Recurrent gene fusions involving YAP1 with MAML2 or NUTM1 have been identified, indicating a shared oncogenic driver across the poroma-porocarcinoma spectrum. Malignant transformation to porocarcinoma involves acquisition of cytological atypia, infiltrative growth and a capacity for lymphatic and distant spread.
additionalInvestigations: dermoscopy to characterise the vascular pattern
immunohistochemistry demonstrating ductal (EMA/CEA) differentiation where required
sentinel lymph node assessment if porocarcinoma is confirmed
staging imaging when malignancy with metastatic potential is diagnosed
redFlags: rapid growth, ulceration or bleeding suggesting porocarcinoma
an infiltrative, indurated or fixed lesion
regional lymphadenopathy indicating possible metastatic porocarcinoma
reference.prognosis: Benign poroma is cured by complete excision with a low recurrence rate. Porocarcinoma carries a less favourable outlook, with potential for local recurrence and lymphatic or distant metastasis, so early recognition is important.
pitfalls: Mistaking a bleeding vascular poroma for a pyogenic granuloma and destroying it without histology.
Overlooking porocarcinoma arising within a long-standing poroma that suddenly changes.
Failing to excise completely, allowing recurrence.
Confusing the lesion with a plantar wart and applying inappropriate keratolytic or destructive therapy.
management: Treat the benign poroma with complete surgical excision, which is curative with a low recurrence rate
Confirm the diagnosis histologically and distinguish it from porocarcinoma, pyogenic granuloma and amelanotic melanoma
If porocarcinoma is confirmed, perform wide local excision with clear margins, or Mohs micrographic surgery for anatomically critical sites
Arrange sentinel lymph node assessment and staging imaging when malignant transformation with metastatic potential is diagnosed
Refer to dermatology or plastic surgery for excision, and to oncology for porocarcinoma with nodal or distant spread
Provide clinical follow-up for local recurrence and, in porocarcinoma, for lymphatic or distant metastasis
